title: The Call of Abram and a Detour into Egypt
summary: The LORD calls Abram to leave his country and family for a land he will be shown, promising to make him a great nation, to bless him, to make his name great, and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abram obeys at seventy-five, travels through Canaan, and builds altars at Shechem and near Bethel after God promises the land to his offspring. When famine strikes he goes down to Egypt, where fear leads him to pass Sarai off as his sister; she is taken into Pharaoh's palace until the LORD strikes Pharaoh's house with plagues, and Pharaoh sends Abram away.
story: This is the hinge of Genesis and, in a real sense, of the whole Bible. Chapters 1 to 11 told the story of all humanity and ended with sin spreading, curse multiplying, and the nations scattered after Babel. Now God answers the whole world's problem by speaking to one man. The promises of verses 1 to 3 set the agenda for everything that follows: offspring, land, and blessing for the nations. Israel's history, the kingdom of David, the prophets' hopes, and the mission of the church all trace back to this call. Yet the chapter does not end in triumph. Within a few verses the man of promise is in Egypt, lying to protect himself and endangering the very wife through whom the promised offspring must come. God's promise, not Abram's character, carries the story forward.
historical:
The stories of Abram have traditionally been placed in the early second millennium BC, though dating them is contested, and some scholars regard them as later compositions (see the introduction). Semi-nomadic herders moving between Mesopotamia, Canaan, and Egypt were a familiar part of that world. A well-known painting in the tomb of the Egyptian official Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan, from around 1900 BC, shows a group of colorfully dressed travelers from western Asia arriving in Egypt with their animals. When rain failed in Canaan, Egypt, watered by the Nile's yearly flood rather than by rain, was the natural place to find food.

The king of Egypt is called Pharaoh, a title that means great house and was used for the king from the second half of the second millennium BC; Genesis never gives his name. The mention of camels in verse 16 has been debated. A 2014 study of camel bones from copper mines in the Aravah valley suggested that domesticated camels became common in the region only around the tenth century BC, and some scholars take the reference as a detail from a later age. Others argue that camels were known and used in smaller numbers much earlier. The places Abram visits (Shechem, Bethel, Ai, and the Negev in the dry south) are real sites that later become central to Israel's history.
cultural:
Leaving one's country, kindred, and father's household was a staggering request in the ancient world. The household was a person's security, identity, and inheritance; to leave it was to become a resident alien, dependent on the goodwill of strangers. Abram does exactly that, and the chapter shows him living as an outsider in a land already occupied. The Oak of Moreh (the name may mean teacher) was probably a well-known tree where people sought oracles, and by building altars at Shechem and near Bethel, Abram marks the land as belonging to the LORD. The comment that the Canaanites were then in the land has long drawn attention; the medieval Jewish commentator Abraham ibn Ezra hinted that it may have been written after the Canaanites were gone.

The episode in Egypt reflects the vulnerability of a foreigner with a beautiful wife. Abram fears that powerful men will kill him to take her. Sarai was in fact his half-sister (20:12), so his words were a half-truth designed to deceive. Rulers in the ancient world took many women into their households, and Pharaoh treats Abram as the family of a new wife, giving him rich gifts as though arranging a marriage. Abram leaves Egypt wealthy, but his wealth was gained at his wife's expense.
literary: The chapter has two parts that sit in sharp tension. Verses 1 to 9 present Abram at his best: God speaks, and Abram goes, without a word of reply. The promise in verses 2 and 3 uses the root for blessing five times, answering the five times the verb to curse has appeared in the chapters before (3:14, 3:17, 4:11, 5:29, and 9:25). The command go (in Hebrew lekh-lekha) will be heard again in Abraham's story only once, in 22:2, when God tells Abraham to go to the land of Moriah, a place God will show him; the two calls frame Abraham's story. Verses 10 to 20 then show Abram at his weakest. The account also previews Israel's later exodus: a famine drives the family down to Egypt, Pharaoh takes what is not his, the LORD strikes Pharaoh with plagues, and the family leaves with great possessions. Pharaoh's question, “What have you done to me?” (verse 18), echoes God's question to Eve in 3:13, but now a pagan king is rebuking the man of promise.

outline.t: Abram obeys and comes to Canaan
The promise of the land and altars at Shechem and Bethel
The LORD's plagues and Pharaoh's rebuke

doctrines.note: Abram's first response to God is simply to go, leaving everything familiar for a land he has not seen, on the strength of God's word. Faith here is not a feeling but obedience to a promise. Yet the same chapter shows faith failing under pressure, as fear leads Abram to deceive. Faith in Scripture is real and imperfect at once.

Though the word covenant does not appear until chapter 15, God's promises here are its foundation: a great nation, a great name, a land, and blessing. These promises are unconditional commitments by God, and the rest of Genesis traces how he keeps them through generations of failure.

God's choice of Abram is not favoritism but strategy. He blesses one family so that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. From its first page, Israel's calling is for the sake of the nations, a purpose the New Testament sees fulfilled in the gospel going to the Gentiles.

When Abram's fear puts Sarai and the promise at risk, the LORD intervenes to protect them. God's purposes do not depend on the faithfulness of the people he has chosen. He guards his promise even when its bearers endanger it.

words.note: Barakh, to bless. To bless is to give life, fruitfulness, and well-being, and to declare someone favored. The verb and its noun appear five times in verses 2 and 3. The last line can be read as all the families of the earth will be blessed through you or will bless themselves by you (that is, invoke your name in blessing). The Greek translation and the New Testament take it in the first sense.

Qalal, to be light or to treat lightly, translated curse in verse 3. God uses two different verbs: whoever treats Abram with contempt (qalal) God will curse (arar). The first verb is milder, and in Hebrew the ones who bless are plural while the one who treats Abram lightly is singular, suggesting that blessing is expected to be the rule and contempt the exception.

Gur, to sojourn, to live somewhere as a resident foreigner without the rights of a citizen. Abram goes to Egypt to sojourn there, and the related noun ger, sojourner or stranger, describes the patriarchs' status in Canaan. Israel's later law repeatedly commands care for the stranger because Israel had been strangers in Egypt.

Zera, seed or offspring. In verse 7 God promises the land not to Abram himself but to his offspring, a promise that immediately raises a problem, since Sarai is barren (11:30). The word continues the thread that began in 3:15 and becomes the heart of the promises to Abraham.

christ: The New Testament treats this chapter as the first announcement of the gospel to the nations. Paul writes that “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: All nations will be blessed through you” (Galatians 3:8), and he concludes that “those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (Galatians 3:9). Christ, he says, redeemed us “in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:14). Peter preached the same promise in the temple, reminding his hearers that God said to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring (Acts 3:25), and then announcing that God had raised up his Servant to bless them. Matthew begins his Gospel by calling Jesus “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). Hebrews holds up the moment of Abram's departure as a model of faith: he “obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). The promise to bless all families finds its fulfillment in Christ, through whom people of every nation are welcomed into Abraham's family.

hard.q: Why does Abram lie about Sarai, and why does Pharaoh suffer for it?
hard.a:
Only a few verses after trusting God enough to leave everything, Abram trusts his own scheme to survive in Egypt. He asks Sarai to say she is his sister, a half-truth, so that he will be spared and treated well. The result is that Sarai is taken into Pharaoh's household, and the promise that depends on her is put at risk. The narrator does not excuse Abram. He lets Pharaoh, the outsider, deliver the rebuke, and Abram has no answer. Interpreters have judged him differently. The medieval Jewish commentator Nachmanides considered his actions a serious sin, both in endangering his wife and in leaving the land out of fear. Others have been gentler, noting the real danger he faced. The fact that he repeats the same scheme in chapter 20, and Isaac copies it in chapter 26, suggests the text sees it as a pattern of fearful self-protection rather than wisdom.

Pharaoh's suffering raises its own question, since he acted without knowing Sarai was married. The text says the plagues came because of Sarai. The best reading is that God acted to protect Sarai and the promise, and that the plagues were the means by which Pharaoh discovered the truth and released her. The point is not that Pharaoh was more guilty than Abram, but that God will not let his promise be lost, even when its bearer puts it in jeopardy.

questions: Abram left his country, family, and security on the strength of God's promise. What would it cost you to take a step of obedience where you cannot see the outcome?
God blesses Abram so that he will be a blessing to all families of the earth. How might you see your own blessings as meant for the sake of others?
The man who trusted God to leave home then trusted his own scheme in Egypt. Where are you tempted to protect yourself in ways that put others at risk?
